item.title: A pretend radio station goes online
item.dc:creator: Global Voices Central & Eastern Europe
item.content:encoded:
A small station finds new listeners

Originally published on Global Voices

A radio studio. Image from Flickr. CC BY-NC-ND 2.0.

For many years a small radio station was one of the few places where people could hear their own language on air. Older listeners tuned in every evening, but younger people spent more and more time on their phones, and the team began to worry that the station would lose them.

So the team decided to record podcasts and put them online. They learned to edit sound on cheap laptops, invited guests from the neighbourhood, and asked teenagers what they wanted to hear. The first episodes were about music, food and family stories, and they were shared widely in group chats.

What changed

Within a year the station had more listeners than before, and many of them were under thirty. Teachers started to use the episodes in class, and parents said that their children asked questions about old words and songs that nobody had explained to them before.

The next challenge is money. The project was paid for by a small grant, and the team now needs a way to keep going after it ends. They are talking to local businesses and to other stations that want to try the same idea in their own languages and towns.

This post is part of a pretend Spotlight series about local media.

item.title: A pretend partner story about city heat
item.dc:creator: Guest Contributor
item.content:encoded:
By A. Writer

This article was originally published by A Partner Newsroom on May 10, 2026, and an edited version is republished here with permission. It is also part of a pretend Spotlight series about climate and cities, which looks at how people adapt.

Residents of a hot city plant trees and gardens to cool their streets during the long summer months, and neighbours share water and seeds.
